title: Write requirements you can verify
subtitle: Turn a vague request into an observable obligation. Then prove you can use the method.
audience: Adults new to requirements writing. No systems engineering background required.

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Appendix C
sources.section: C.1; C.2 Product Requirement; C.4 Clarity and Verifiability/Testability
sources.claim: A requirement names its responsible product, states one obligation, and supports an objective compliance check. Ambiguous terms and unjustified assumptions weaken it.
sources.limits: Selected guidance, not a complete requirements standard or approval checklist. Local project rules and justified design constraints still apply.

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Product Verification
sources.section: 5.3 Product Verification, introduction and process description
sources.claim: Verification compares a realized product with its specified requirements using planned evidence. Inspection, analysis, demonstration, and test can contribute.
sources.limits: The appropriate evidence method depends on the requirement and product. A measurement example here is not a full test procedure.

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook — Product Validation
sources.section: 5.4 Product Validation, introduction and process description
sources.claim: Product validation examines whether the product fulfills its intended use and stakeholder expectations in the relevant environment.
sources.limits: Passing a specified threshold alone does not establish fitness for the real use. Requirements validation and product validation are distinct activities.

content_notice: Original instructional examples and exercises informed by the linked NASA guidance. All numerical thresholds and project facts are invented teaching assumptions, not NASA requirements. No endorsement or certification is implied.

concepts.title: One clear obligation
concepts.objective: Identify the responsible product and separate independent obligations.
concepts.explanation: Name the product and its required behavior. Split obligations that can pass or fail independently. Put the reason for a requirement in a separate rationale.
concepts.misconception: Adding “shall” does not make an ambiguous or compound sentence verifiable.

example.before: The desk service should be helpful and notify users and keep records.
example.after: DESK-01: The desk service shall send a receipt to the requester after accepting a support request.
example.why: This isolates one behavior. Receipt content and delivery timing still need separate agreed criteria; this sentence is not yet a finished baseline.

diagnostic.prompt: A draft says: “The station display shall show departures and archive maintenance logs.” What is the first useful repair?

choices.text: Split display behavior from log retention.
choices.feedback: Yes. Each obligation can fail while the other succeeds. Separate them before defining detailed acceptance criteria.

choices.text: Replace “shall” with “will.”
choices.feedback: Changing the verb does not resolve the two independent obligations.

choices.text: Add “reliably” to the end.
choices.feedback: “Reliably” adds no measurable criterion and leaves both obligations tangled.

diagnostic.hint: Could one part pass while the other fails?

practice.prompt: Which draft isolates one product obligation?

choices.text: The sensor shall log readings, email alerts, and stay easy to maintain.
choices.feedback: This combines logging, notification, and a vague maintenance goal.

choices.text: The sensor shall record a timestamp with each accepted reading.
choices.feedback: Yes. One product performs one observable behavior. The timestamp format can be specified next.

choices.text: The operator will probably review the readings.
choices.feedback: This describes an uncertain human activity, not a sensor obligation.

practice.hint: Find one named product and one observable behavior.

transfer.prompt: A library kiosk must print a receipt and erase a patron’s temporary session data. Why write two requirements?

choices.text: To make the document look more detailed.
choices.feedback: Document length does not justify decomposition.

choices.text: Because every sentence must have a numerical threshold.
choices.feedback: Not every requirement needs a number; some use observable states or content rules.

choices.text: Because printing and erasure need independently checked outcomes.
choices.feedback: Yes. A printed receipt does not show that temporary data was erased.

transfer.hint: Imagine the receipt prints correctly but data remains.

review.prompt: A new draft says: “The pump shall report pressure and alert an operator when pressure is low.” What do you check first?

choices.text: Whether reporting and alerting have separate acceptance evidence.
choices.feedback: Yes. Distinct outcomes need clear boundaries and evidence.

choices.text: Whether both verbs use the same number of letters.
choices.feedback: Word shape does not affect the required behavior.

choices.text: Whether “intelligently” would make the requirement stronger.
choices.feedback: A descriptive adverb does not resolve the obligations.

writing.prompt: A meeting-room service must confirm bookings and remove cancelled bookings from the room display. Write two separate product requirements. Leave unknown timing as an explicit open issue instead of inventing a promise.

criteria.text: Each statement names the responsible product.
Each statement contains one independently checkable obligation.
Unknown criteria are named as open issues, not hidden assumptions.

writing.example: ROOM-01: The booking service shall send a confirmation to the requester after accepting a booking. ROOM-02: The room display shall remove a booking after receiving its cancellation. Open issues: agree timing and confirmation content with the service owner.
writing.notes: Compare your wording against the criteria. Many answers are valid. This self-check does not approve an engineering baseline.

concepts.title: Make the outcome observable
concepts.objective: Specify an observable result, conditions, and a defensible acceptance boundary.
concepts.explanation: Replace vague performance words with an observable result and its conditions. Choose a threshold only when the scenario supplies it or its owner has agreed it. Record unresolved values explicitly.
concepts.misconception: An exact number is not evidence that the number is justified.

example.before: The desk service shall respond quickly.
example.after: Teaching assumption: the service owner agrees a 5-second receipt target. DESK-02: When an online request is accepted, the desk service shall deliver its receipt within 5 seconds of acceptance.
example.why: A tester can compare the acceptance and receipt timestamps. The assumed target needs validation before real use.

diagnostic.prompt: The owner asks for a “fast” receipt but gives no timing target. What should you do?

choices.text: Declare a 10-millisecond target because it is precise.
choices.feedback: Precision does not justify a target or prove feasibility.

choices.text: Agree a justified timing target and conditions with the owner.
choices.feedback: Yes. Resolve the missing criterion and its basis instead of quietly inventing it.

choices.text: Accept “fast” because everyone understands it.
choices.feedback: Different readers can interpret “fast” differently.

diagnostic.hint: Where does the proposed acceptance threshold come from?

practice.prompt: Teaching assumption: an owner agrees that offline events must be uploaded within 60 seconds after connectivity returns. Which draft is checkable?

choices.text: The client shall upload offline events soon.
choices.feedback: “Soon” has no agreed test boundary.

choices.text: The client shall upload offline events as appropriate.
choices.feedback: “As appropriate” leaves the triggering conditions unspecified.

choices.text: After connectivity returns, the client shall upload its queued offline events within 60 seconds.
choices.feedback: Yes. The condition, result, and time boundary come from the stated assumption.

practice.hint: Use the supplied condition and threshold.

transfer.prompt: A luggage counter must update within 2 seconds after a scan. What evidence directly checks that timing?

choices.text: The scanner’s purchase invoice.
choices.feedback: Purchase evidence does not measure response time.

choices.text: The difference between scan and counter-update timestamps under the specified conditions.
choices.feedback: Yes. Observe the defined trigger and result using an adequate time measurement method.

choices.text: A user saying the counter looks modern.
choices.feedback: Appearance does not establish timing compliance.

transfer.hint: Measure the interval named in the requirement.

review.prompt: An invented scenario specifies a temperature reading within ±0.5 °C at 20 °C. Which result violates that requirement?

choices.feedback: This is 0.2 °C above the reference and inside the stated boundary.
This is 0.4 °C below the reference and inside the stated boundary.
Yes. The error is +0.7 °C, beyond the supplied ±0.5 °C criterion.

review.hint: Compare absolute error with the supplied tolerance.

writing.prompt: Teaching assumption: after a parcel scan is accepted, its status must appear on the operator display within 3 seconds. Write the requirement and describe what you would measure.

criteria.text: The timing starts at scan acceptance.
The result is the parcel status appearing on the operator display.
The 3-second limit is present and attributed to the scenario.
The check compares acceptance and display timestamps.

writing.example: PARCEL-01: After a parcel scan is accepted, the operator display shall show that parcel’s updated status within 3 seconds. Compare the acceptance and display timestamps using a measurement method suited to this limit. The limit is a teaching assumption.
writing.notes: Real verification planning also defines instrumentation, conditions, sample coverage, and uncertainty. This exercise covers the basic evidence link.

concepts.title: Check the promise and the purpose
concepts.objective: Distinguish evidence of requirement compliance from evidence of useful operation.
concepts.explanation: Check compliance with the specified requirement, then examine intended use. These questions need different evidence even when one trial contributes to both.
concepts.misconception: A product can meet a stated requirement while failing the actual user need.

example.before: The receipt arrives within 5 seconds, so the service is useful.
example.after: Verification: measure receipt timing. Product validation: observe whether requesters can use the receipt to track the right request in their real workflow.
example.why: Fast delivery alone does not establish that the receipt helps the requester.

diagnostic.prompt: A booking receipt passes its timing test, but users cannot identify the room it confirms. What follows?

choices.text: The timing requirement may pass while the intended use remains unmet.
choices.feedback: Yes. The evidence answers the timing question, not every user-need question.

choices.text: Passing timing proves the full service is useful.
choices.feedback: The timing result does not establish that users can identify their booking.

choices.text: Verification should be abandoned.
choices.feedback: Compliance checks remain useful; they need complementary evidence about use.

diagnostic.hint: What exactly did the timing test establish?

practice.prompt: Which activity directly examines intended use?

choices.text: Checking the software version string.
choices.feedback: Version identification supports configuration control, not this use claim.

choices.text: Watching representative users identify and reach their booked room using the confirmation.
choices.feedback: Yes. The activity examines the outcome in a relevant user workflow.

choices.text: Counting the number of requirement pages.
choices.feedback: Document size does not establish fitness for use.

practice.hint: Observe the user outcome that motivated the system.

transfer.prompt: A flood-warning display updates within its specified interval, but its symbols confuse operators in a drill. What is the useful next step?

choices.text: Claim complete success based on update timing.
choices.feedback: This would generalize beyond the evidence.

choices.text: Remove the timing requirement from the report.
choices.feedback: A real timing result should be retained with its proper scope.

choices.text: Keep the timing result and investigate operator understanding in the intended context.
choices.feedback: Yes. Preserve the supported result and investigate the unmet operational need.

transfer.hint: Keep supported evidence; name what it does not establish.

review.prompt: A warehouse route planner meets a computation-time limit. Workers still cannot follow its route instructions. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: All requirements must be wrong.
choices.feedback: One unmet use need does not invalidate every requirement.

choices.text: The speed check passed; useful route guidance needs separate evidence.
choices.feedback: Yes. Separate the supported compliance claim from the unresolved use claim.

choices.text: Workers should be excluded from evaluation.
choices.feedback: Representative users are relevant to evaluating intended use.

review.hint: Distinguish measured compliance from useful operation.

writing.prompt: A community centre replaces its sign-in desk with a kiosk. Teaching assumption: it must issue a visitor pass within 15 seconds after a valid sign-in. Write one verification check and one product-validation scenario.

criteria.text: Verification checks the specified 15-second interval and trigger.
Validation observes a representative visitor completing the intended sign-in workflow.
The answer does not equate a timing pass with complete operational success.

writing.example: Verification: measure from accepted valid sign-in to pass issuance and compare with 15 seconds. Product validation: observe representative visitors locating the kiosk, signing in, and using the issued pass to reach the intended activity, including accessibility needs. Retain issues even if timing passes.
writing.notes: These are original teaching scenarios. They do not replace a project validation plan or stakeholder acceptance.
